issues.item: Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively
issues.explanation: Compulsive exercise is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The other selected items cluster around hypervigilance, dissociation, memory disorganisation, and danger-based appraisals after terrorism. Excessive exercise does not clearly serve or connect to those symptoms, making it look like a strategy for a different presentation unless additional context were present.

issues.item: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: 'Life Not Worth Living' is disproportionately severe relative to the rest of the selected profile and is not well supported by the surrounding appraisals. The other appraisals focus on danger and bodily unreliability, while the threat/memory items emphasize hyperarousal and fragmented recall. This suicidal-hopelessness appraisal can occur in PTSD, but here it stands out as insufficiently linked to the rest of the formulation and item set.

vignette:
Marisol is a 24-year-old warehouse worker who came to treatment months after surviving a terrorist bombing at a crowded bus terminal she used every day to get to work. She had finished an early shift and was standing inside the terminal among commuters, looking up for her bus, when the blast went off. What remains most vivid to her is not a coherent sequence but sharp fragments: a violent force through her chest, people dropping, the sound changing all at once, and bodies moving in ways that still feel wrong to her now-jerking, running, falling, grabbing. There are stretches she cannot account for. She knows she got out, knows she was later told she had been found disoriented and shaking, but there are parts she cannot remember no matter how hard she tries. When she does try, she often stops in frustration because the memories come as pieces and sensations rather than words. She will say she knows what happened, then go quiet, jaw tight, unable to describe it. At other moments remembering brings up a burst of rage so intense it scares her, a fury at the people who did it and at the fact that ordinary strangers had been turned into targets on an ordinary afternoon.

In the weeks afterward, Marisol found herself moving through the world as if danger had become its basic rule. She had come to believe that nowhere public was truly safe and that staying alert was the only sensible way to live. At work in the warehouse, where forklifts pass quickly and coworkers round corners carrying boxes, she is constantly scanning the floor, the loading dock, the entrances, and other people's hands and movements. A pallet dropping unexpectedly or someone stepping suddenly into her path puts her immediately on guard. Her body reacts before she can think; she startles hard, shoulders jumping, heart racing. Sudden movements are especially difficult. If a coworker reaches past her without warning, she stiffens and pivots as if bracing for impact. She does not experience this as an overreaction. To her it feels necessary, proof that she is paying attention in a world where terrible things can happen without warning.

She also no longer feels she can trust her own body. The blast taught her, in her mind, that her body can freeze, shake, disappear from her, or fail to protect her. Since then, when she feels overwhelmed, she sometimes deliberately tries to blank out. During a stressful shift or when a memory starts pressing in, she lets herself go distant, as if leaving her body is the fastest way to get through the next few minutes. She knows this can happen while someone is talking to her, and afterward she may realize she missed instructions or has to ask for something to be repeated. That loss of control frightens her almost as much as the memories themselves.

Her relationships at work have changed in small, cumulative ways. Marisol avoids eye contact, especially with men she does not know well or with anyone approaching her too quickly. Coworkers have sometimes read this as rudeness or distraction. She keeps conversations short and prefers tasks she can do without much interaction. If the team takes breaks together, she often chooses a seat where she can watch the door and the whole room. Night is markedly worse. She finds it much harder to feel safe after dark, and even in her apartment she becomes more alert to every sound outside, every footstep in the hallway, every car door slamming below her window. What frightens her most is the sense that danger moves fastest when visibility is low and people are less prepared.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was exhausted from living in this state of readiness. The final push came after a late shift when a coworker came up behind her near the loading area and waved to get her attention. The sudden movement made her spin around and recoil so sharply that she dropped what she was carrying. She felt embarrassed, angry, and then strangely far away from herself, as if she had vanished mid-scene. Afterward she sat in her car unable to put into words why she was shaking so badly. She came to therapy because she does not want her life to keep narrowing around watchfulness, silence, and fear. At the same time, she is afraid that if she lets her guard down, even a little, something catastrophic will happen again, and afraid too of what might come back if she ever stops forcing herself to go blank.
